description: I'm PitcheEshwar, a student from Chennai, India, building "The Earth Information Jukebox," a web app that turns NASA Earth data into real-time sound so people can hear climate change as well as see it. My skills include [JavaScript, Python, UI design], and I'm interested in accessibility, data visualization and audio. I'm looking for teammates with frontend (Web Audio API), data handling, UI design or sound design skills, and beginners are welcome.
summary:
Challenge: The Earth Information Jukebox (NASA Space Apps 2026). Team Sole Sword, solo builder Pitche Eshwar R.

Problem: Earth science is shared mostly through maps and charts, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. At least 2.2 billion people have a vision impairment (WHO).

Solution: A web app that turns NASA’s global temperature record from 1880 to 2025 into sound. Warmer years sound higher, and a chart cursor moves in sync. The whole record plays in about 29 seconds.
How it works:

Data is NASA GISS GISTEMP v4, with 146 annual and 1,752 monthly values.
Pitch = 220 Hz × 4^((anomaly − min) / (max − min)), which maps −0.5 to +1.3 °C onto two octaves (220–880 Hz).
Built with plain JavaScript, the Web Audio API and an SVG chart. There is no backend, login or paid service.

What makes it understandable: reference tones, a chime on every record-high year, a plain-language sentence for each point, a stereo sweep as time passes, and keyboard and screen-reader support.

What the data sounds like:

The pitch climbs about 1.6 octaves, from 284 Hz in 1880 to 866 Hz in 2024.
There are 22 record-high years, 14 of them in 1980 or later.
The warming trend is +0.21 °C per decade since 1975, against +0.08 over the whole record.
details:
Here is a version you can paste directly (about 380 words):

What it does and how it works: Earth Jukebox turns NASA's global temperature record into sound, so people can hear climate change as well as see it. It uses NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 data from 1880 to 2025 (146 annual and 1,752 monthly values). Each temperature anomaly, measured against the 1951–1980 average, becomes one musical pitch: warmer years sound higher. The rule is pitch = 220 Hz × 4^((a − min) / (max − min)), so the range of −0.5 to +1.3 °C maps onto two octaves (220–880 Hz), and equal temperature steps sound like equal musical steps. A chart cursor moves in sync with the sound. The full record plays in about 29 seconds, and users can choose annual or monthly data, a year range, speed and volume.

Benefits and intended impact: Most Earth science is shared through maps and charts, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. The WHO reports at least 2.2 billion people with a near or distance vision impairment. Our aim is to make NASA's Earth data reachable for them, and to give teachers, museums and science centres a free audio tool for climate education.

Tools used: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in a single page; the Web Audio API for sound; SVG for the synced chart; Python for preparing the data and independent checks. It needs no server, login or paid service. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant for code, slides and writing, and checked all figures against the data and the cited sources.

Creativity: Beyond playing data as tones, we added reference tones (baseline, coolest, warmest) so listeners learn the scale first, a bell chime on every record-high year, a stereo sweep from left to right as time passes, and a plain-language sentence explaining each point. Users can also load NASA's own latest file.

Factors we considered: accuracy (a fixed pitch range, so a short clip sounds the same as the full playback, with the mapping and data source shown on screen); understanding (research on NASA sonifications found many listeners misread pitch, so we explain every sound); accessibility (keyboard control, screen-reader announcements, visible focus); and simplicity (one free web page that works anywhere). Current limits: it shows global averages with a chart, not yet Earth Information Center images or regional views, and it still needs testing with blind and low-vision users. Next steps are user testing, regional data starting with India, and pilots with schools and science centres.
